Predicting Where Steering Vectors Succeed

Jayadev Billa ††thanks: Unaffiliated researcher; previously at ISI@USC, Yahoo, Nuance, and BBN. Email: jbilla2004@gmail.com
Abstract

Steering vectors work for some concepts and layers but fail for others, and practitioners have no way to predict which setting applies before running an intervention. We introduce the Linear Accessibility Profile (lap), a per-layer diagnostic that repurposes the logit lens as a predictor of steering vector effectiveness. The key measure, AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}, applies the model’s unembedding matrix to intermediate hidden states, requiring no training. Across 24 controlled binary concept families on five models (Pythia-2.8B to Llama-8B), peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} predicts steering effectiveness at ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 to +0.91+0.91 and layer selection at ρ=+0.63\rho=+0.63 to +0.92+0.92. A three-regime framework explains when difference-of-means steering works, when nonlinear methods are needed, and when no method can work. An entity-steering demo confirms the prediction end-to-end: steering at the lap-recommended layer redirects completions on Gemma-2-2B and OLMo-2-1B-Instruct, while the middle layer (the standard heuristic) has no effect on either model.

1 Introduction

Steering vectors add a direction to the residual stream to shift model behavior. They have been applied to refusal (Arditi et al., 2024), truthfulness (Li et al., 2023), and broader behavioral properties (Zou et al., 2023; Turner et al., 2023). However, effectiveness varies across concepts and layers, and practitioners currently select steering layers by trial and error. No systematic method predicts which setting will succeed.

The logit lens (nostalgebraist, 2020) applies the unembedding matrix to intermediate hidden states to observe how predictions evolve across layers. Belrose et al. (2023) addressed the layer norm mismatch with a learned correction (the “tuned lens”). These methods characterize what the model “thinks” at each layer, but none connects this measurement to the success or failure of steering interventions.

We repurpose the logit lens as a predictor of steering vector effectiveness. The resulting framework, the Linear Accessibility Profile (lap), measures at each layer whether a concept is accessible through the model’s own output projection and whether that accessibility predicts where steering will work. Prior work selects steering layers heuristically, typically targeting middle layers (Turner et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024). lap operates at a different level: predicting whether a concept is steerable at all. A concept with high peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} (e.g., continent, Alin=0.68A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0.68) steers effectively; one with low peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} (e.g., parity, Alin=0.02A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0.02) does not. We complement the logit lens with a nonlinear upper bound (a residual MLP) to quantify the probe gap, and measure perturbation sensitivity (λ\lambda) to identify layers where the representation is unstable.

We validate lap on single-token next-token completion tasks, where the logit lens gives an unambiguous accuracy metric. Extensions to multi-token settings are discussed in Section 5. We evaluate primarily on Gemma-2-2B (Gemma Team, 2024) and replicate on Llama-3.1-8B (Dubey et al., 2024), Mistral-7B-v0.3, Qwen2.5-7B, and two non-transformers (Mamba-1.4B, RWKV-1.6B). An entity-steering demo validates lap end-to-end: steering London-answer prompts toward “Paris” at the lap-recommended layer redirects completions on both Gemma-2-2B and OLMo-2-1B-Instruct, while the middle layer has no effect on either model.

Our contributions: (1) a connection between logit lens measurements and steering vector effectiveness, validated at two levels (layer selection and steerability prediction) across 24 controlled families and five models; (2) a three-regime framework that explains when difference-of-means steering works, when nonlinear methods are needed, and when no method can work; (3) a controlled experimental design using 25 binary concept families that isolates representation geometry from task-structure confounds.

2 Related Work

The logit lens and probing.

nostalgebraist (2020) introduced the logit lens; Belrose et al. (2023) proposed the tuned lens to address the layer norm mismatch; Yom Din et al. (2023) examined how predictions change at certain layers. We show that the standard logit lens, despite the mismatch, is a strong predictor of steering effectiveness. By using the model’s own unembedding (a fixed, untrained projection), we avoid the selectivity concerns that apply to trained probes (Belinkov, 2022). The trade-off is that we measure alignment with one specific linear projection, not general linear decodability.

Linear representations.

Park et al. (2024) formalize the linear representation hypothesis and connect it to probing and steering. Nanda et al. (2023) observe linear representations in Othello-playing models. The hypothesis has been challenged: Csordás et al. (2024) show nonlinear encodings in small models, and Engels et al. (2024) demonstrate multi-dimensional feature manifolds. We do not assume the hypothesis holds universally; lap measures where and to what degree it holds.

Steering and intervention.

Zou et al. (2023) introduce representation engineering. Turner et al. (2023) formalize activation addition. Arditi et al. (2024) identify a single direction mediating refusal. Each method demonstrates success on its target concept but does not predict when steering will succeed on a new concept or layer.

Sparse autoencoders and transcoders.

Templeton et al. (2024) scale SAEs to large models; Lieberum et al. (2024) release GemmaScope transcoders; Ameisen et al. (2025) introduce attribution graphs. Our three-regime framework predicts that SAE features should be most useful in regime 2 (concept present but not output-aligned), where difference-of-means fails.

3 Method

3.1 Setup

Consider a causal language model with LL transformer blocks. Each block reads from and writes to a shared residual stream: hℓ=hℓ−1+blockℓ​(hℓ−1)h_{\ell}=h_{\ell-1}+\mathrm{block}_{\ell}(h_{\ell-1}), where h0h_{0} is the token embedding. After the final block, an output head11 1 All transformer models in this paper use RMSNorm rather than standard LayerNorm. We write LayerNorm throughout for readability; the distinction does not affect the logit lens analysis. produces logits: logits=WU⋅LayerNorm​(hL)\mathrm{logits}=W_{U}\cdot\text{LayerNorm}(h_{L}), where WU∈ℝV×dW_{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{V\times d} is the unembedding matrix. Because the residual stream lives in ℝd\mathbb{R}^{d} at every layer, this output head can be applied to any intermediate hℓh_{\ell}, which is the basis of the logit lens.

For a concept family 𝒞={(xi,ti)}i=1N\mathcal{C}=\{(x_{i},t_{i})\}_{i=1}^{N}, where each prompt xix_{i} has a correct next-token answer tit_{i}, we measure how linearly accessible the concept is at each layer.

3.2 Linear accuracy (logit lens)

We apply the model’s unembedding to intermediate hidden states:

Alin​(ℓ)=1N​∑i=1N{1if ​arg⁡maxv​(WU⋅LayerNorm​(hℓ(i)))v=ti0otherwiseA_{\mathrm{lin}}(\ell)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\arg\max_{v}(W_{U}\cdot\text{LayerNorm}(h_{\ell}^{(i)}))_{v}=t_{i}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (1)

This is the logit lens evaluated as classification accuracy over the concept family. No training is required. We apply the final layer norm to intermediate states, inheriting the layer norm mismatch discussed by Belrose et al. (2023). We evaluate the effect of this mismatch in Section 5.

3.3 Probe gap

The logit lens measures what is linearly accessible through the model’s output projection, but concept information may be present in a form that requires nonlinear transformation before it aligns with the unembedding. The probe gap Δ⁡(ℓ)=Amlp​(ℓ)−Alin​(ℓ)\Delta(\ell)=A_{\mathrm{mlp}}(\ell)-A_{\mathrm{lin}}(\ell) quantifies how much concept information is present at layer ℓ\ell but not output-aligned.

We train a residual MLP to compute AmlpA_{\mathrm{mlp}}:

h^ℓ=hℓ+fθ​(hℓ),Amlp​(ℓ)=1N​∑i=1N{1if ​arg⁡maxv​(WU⋅LayerNorm​(h^ℓ(i)))v=ti0otherwise\hat{h}_{\ell}=h_{\ell}+f_{\theta}(h_{\ell}),\qquad A_{\mathrm{mlp}}(\ell)=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\begin{cases}1&\text{if }\arg\max_{v}(W_{U}\cdot\text{LayerNorm}(\hat{h}_{\ell}^{(i)}))_{v}=t_{i}\\ 0&\text{otherwise}\end{cases} (2)

where fθf_{\theta} is a two-layer MLP (d→512→dd\to 512\to d) with layer normalization, GELU, and dropout (p=0.1p=0.1), trained on 80% of prompts to minimize cross-entropy. The residual connection ensures the MLP learns a correction rather than replacing the hidden state. A large probe gap indicates nonlinear encoding at that layer; steering is unlikely to work even though the information is present.

3.4 Perturbation sensitivity

We measure how much a small random perturbation at layer ℓ\ell is amplified by subsequent computation:

λ⁡(ℓ)=1K​∑k=1K‖f⁡(hℓ+α​ϵk)−f⁡(hℓ)‖α,α=0.01⋅‖hℓ‖\lambda(\ell)=\frac{1}{K}\sum_{k=1}^{K}\frac{\|f(h_{\ell}+\alpha\epsilon_{k})-f(h_{\ell})\|}{\alpha},\qquad\alpha=0.01\cdot\|h_{\ell}\| (3)

where ϵk\epsilon_{k} are random unit vectors, ff is the forward pass from layer ℓ\ell to output logits, and K=10K=10. High λ\lambda indicates an unstable representation where steering vectors will have unpredictable effects.

3.5 The Linear Accessibility Profile

For a concept family 𝒞\mathcal{C} and layer ℓ\ell, the Linear Accessibility Profile (lap) is:

lap​(ℓ)=(Alin​(ℓ),Δ⁡(ℓ),λ⁡(ℓ))\textsc{lap}(\ell)=\bigl(A_{\mathrm{lin}}(\ell),\;\Delta(\ell),\;\lambda(\ell)\bigr) (4)

Of these, AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is the primary predictor. The remaining components characterize why steering may fail: high Δ\Delta means information is present but not output-aligned; high λ\lambda means the representation is unstable (Figure 3 in Appendix K).

3.6 Concept families

We use two sets of concept families. All correct answers are single tokens in the model vocabulary (required because the logit lens produces a distribution over individual tokens).

Core families (5).

Five heterogeneous families (Table 1) are used for within-concept analyses: measuring how AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}, Δ\Delta, and λ\lambda vary across layers for a single concept.

Controlled binary families (25).

For steerability prediction across concepts, task-structure confounds must be eliminated. The core families vary in answer-class count, target sizes, and prompt formats; comparing steerability across them yields a non-significant correlation (ρ=+0.18\rho=+0.18, p=0.54p=0.54). We construct 25 controlled binary families (Table 14 in the appendix): each has two answer classes, balanced groups (∼\sim22 items per class), and consistent templates. This reveals the underlying signal (ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 to +0.91+0.91, p<10−3p<10^{-3}; details in Appendix D).

4 Experiments

We evaluate primarily on Gemma-2-2B (26 layers, d=2304d=2304) with replication on Llama-3.1-8B (32 layers), Mistral-7B-v0.3 (32 layers), Qwen2.5-7B (28 layers), and two non-transformer architectures: Mamba-1.4B (48 layers) and RWKV-1.6B (24 layers). Table 6 in the appendix specifies which model is used for each experiment.

4.1 Linear accessibility across layers

Table 2 reports the main results. All five families show zero linear accuracy for layers 0–15 and sharp emergence in layers 18–24, consistent with the logit lens literature (nostalgebraist, 2020; Yom Din et al., 2023). Accuracy peaks at layer 23–24 (not the final layer) for four of five families.

The probe gap varies widely. For arithmetic and sequence, Δ≈0.22\Delta\approx 0.22: the concept is predominantly linear at the best layer. For geography, Δ=0.720\Delta=0.720: the MLP achieves perfect accuracy while the logit lens reaches only 28.0%. The MLP also detects concepts earlier: sequence is nonlinearly accessible at layer 5 (Amlp=0.91A_{\mathrm{mlp}}=0.91) but not linearly until layer 20 (Alin=0.60A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0.60).

Crystallization gap.

We define the gap between nonlinear detection (Amlp>0.5A_{\mathrm{mlp}}>0.5) and linear emergence (Alin>0.1A_{\mathrm{lin}}>0.1) as the crystallization gap. Both metrics measure argmax accuracy over the full vocabulary (∼\sim256K tokens), so chance is effectively zero. The AmlpA_{\mathrm{mlp}} threshold of 50% indicates the nonlinear probe recovers the correct token for a majority of prompts. The AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} threshold is lower at 10% because sporadic values of 1–3% can arise from token frequency biases in the unembedding; 10% requires a substantial fraction of prompts to have the correct token as the logit lens argmax. The gap varies systematically (Table 10 in the appendix): sequence is nonlinearly detectable at layer 1 but not linearly accessible until layer 19, a gap of 18 layers (69% of depth). Word transformation and analogy show the opposite pattern, with AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} emerging before AmlpA_{\mathrm{mlp}} reaches 0.5, suggesting these concepts are natively aligned with the unembedding. Tuned lens comparisons shift emergence 2–5 layers earlier but do not eliminate the gap, confirming that the crystallization gap reflects genuine nonlinear encoding rather than layer norm mismatch alone.

We also observe that AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} tracks the model’s own accuracy. Table 2 splits AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} by whether the model answers each prompt correctly (Acc(a)) or incorrectly (Acc(b)). On prompts where the model’s top-1 prediction is correct, AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} ranges from 0.47 to 0.95; on prompts where the model gets the answer wrong, AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is 0.00 to 0.17. Linear accessibility appears to be a necessary condition for correct output.

4.2 Predicting steering vector effectiveness

For each concept family, we select a target answer (one specific correct token that appears frequently), split prompts into target and non-target groups, compute the steering direction as dℓ=h¯ℓtarget−h¯ℓnon-targetd_{\ell}=\bar{h}_{\ell}^{\,\text{target}}-\bar{h}_{\ell}^{\,\text{non-target}} at each layer, inject dℓd_{\ell} into non-target prompts, and measure the change in target-token probability (Δ​P\Delta P).

Raw correlations.

Table 3 reports Spearman ρ\rho between AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} and Δ​P\Delta P per family. Correlations range from +0.72+0.72 to +0.87+0.87, all p<10−3p<10^{-3}.

Controlling for depth.

Both AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} and Δ​P\Delta P increase with layer depth. The pooled partial correlation controlling for layer index is r=+0.507r=+0.507 (p<10−9p<10^{-9}, n=130n=130); four of five families remain individually significant (Table 3). Details of the restricted analysis and permutation test are in Appendix H.

Steerability prediction.

The more practically important question is whether a concept is steerable at all, and by what method. The full LAP profile identifies three regimes. When AmlpA_{\mathrm{mlp}} is low, the concept is not yet represented in the residual stream and no steering method can work, regardless of technique. When AmlpA_{\mathrm{mlp}} is high but AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is low (the crystallization gap), the concept is present but nonlinearly encoded; difference-of-means steering fails because the separating direction does not align with the output projection, though nonlinear methods such as SAE feature amplification (Templeton et al., 2024) could potentially extract the concept. When AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is high, the concept is output-aligned and difference-of-means steering works. AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} thus serves as a diagnostic for the choice of steering method: it tells the practitioner whether the simpler difference-of-means approach will suffice, or whether a more sophisticated technique is needed.

The standard heuristic is to steer at the middle layer (Turner et al., 2023; Templeton et al., 2024). The three regimes explain both its successes and failures. In our refusal demo on Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (Appendix Q), the refusal direction has separability 0.988 at the middle layer, so difference-of-means works. For factual concepts on Gemma-2-2B, the middle layer is in regime 2: all five families show Amlp>0.7A_{\mathrm{mlp}}>0.7 at L15 but Alin=0A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0 (Figure 1). The concepts are present but not output-aligned, and steering has no effect. Steering works only at late layers (L22 on Gemma, L13 on OLMo) where Alin>0A_{\mathrm{lin}}>0. The Golden Gate Claude result (Templeton et al., 2024) is consistent with regime 2: SAE feature amplification can extract concept information that is present nonlinearly.

AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} provides a concept-specific prediction. Continent has peak Alin=0.70A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0.70 and steers effectively (Δ​P=+0.77\Delta P=+0.77 on Llama-8B); parity-related concepts with peak Alin<0.05A_{\mathrm{lin}}<0.05 do not steer (typical Δ​P<0.01\Delta P<0.01). To test this cleanly, we use the 25 controlled binary families described in Section 3.6.

Across these controlled families (Figure 2), peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} predicts maximum steering Δ​P\Delta P with ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 to +0.91+0.91 across five models (all p<10−3p<10^{-3}). The correlation strengthens with model size and holds above the Alin=0A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0 floor on larger models: restricting to families with Alin>0.1A_{\mathrm{lin}}>0.1, ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 on Qwen-7B (n=13n=13) and ρ=+0.84\rho=+0.84 on Llama-8B (n=14n=14).

The output-alignment principle.

Why does AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} predict steering? Steering adds a direction dd to hℓh_{\ell}, and the model’s readout is approximately linear: C⁡(hℓ+d)≈C⁡(hℓ)+C⁡(d)C(h_{\ell}+d)\approx C(h_{\ell})+C(d), where C=WU∘LayerNormC=W_{U}\circ\text{LayerNorm}. The steering effect is governed by C⁡(d)C(d): the steering direction projected through the unembedding. If C⁡(d)C(d) assigns high weight to the target token, steering shifts probability toward it; if C⁡(d)C(d) points at unrelated tokens, the perturbation produces unpredictable changes. AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} measures exactly this alignment. Empirically, C​(d)targetC(d)_{\mathrm{target}} correlates with Δ​P\Delta P (ρ=+0.73\rho=+0.73 to +0.84+0.84 across three models, all p<10−4p<10^{-4}), and AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is a stronger predictor (ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 to +0.90+0.90) because it captures the concept’s overall organization in the output space.

Collateral damage and steering efficiency.

We define steering efficiency as Δ​P/KLcollateral\Delta P/\mathrm{KL}_{\mathrm{collateral}}, where KLcollateral\mathrm{KL}_{\mathrm{collateral}} measures the KL divergence on 50 unrelated prompts. On Gemma-2-2B, steering at the AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}-recommended layer produces substantially higher efficiency than the middle layer for all five families: sequence is +1.31+1.31 at L24 vs. +0.000+0.000 at L13; arithmetic is +0.84+0.84 vs. +0.094+0.094 (full comparison in Table 18; analysis in Appendix P). Across concepts, peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} correlates with efficiency at ρ=+0.63\rho=+0.63 to +0.65+0.65 across three models (Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-1.5B, Pythia-2.8B; all p<10−3p<10^{-3}).

Cross-model consistency.

Concepts that are linearly separable in one model’s output space should be linearly separable in another trained on similar data. We observe this: AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} on Gemma predicts Δ​P\Delta P on Qwen-7B (ρ=+0.85\rho=+0.85) and Llama-8B (ρ=+0.88\rho=+0.88), nearly as strong as same-model prediction. A practitioner can screen concepts on a cheap model: AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} on Qwen-1.5B predicts Δ​P\Delta P on Llama-8B (ρ=+0.85\rho=+0.85) and Qwen-7B (ρ=+0.88\rho=+0.88).

Scaling with model size.

Across five Pythia models (160M to 6.9B), mean peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} increases with scale (0.055 to 0.118) and the number of steerable concepts grows (5/23 to 9/23). Mean steering Δ​P\Delta P increases roughly 3.4×3.4\times (0.011 to 0.037). Both AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} and the steerable count plateau between 2.8B and 6.9B. The cross-family correlation ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P)\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P) strengthens with scale (+0.42+0.42 at 160M to +0.86+0.86 at 6.9B; Table 16), suggesting the diagnostic becomes more informative on larger models.

Layer selection and trained probe failure.

Steering at the highest-AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} layer matches or near-matches the oracle for 4 of 5 families (Table 11 in the appendix). A trained logistic regression probe achieves >>93% classification accuracy at every layer from L0 to L25, yet steering at early layers produces zero Δ​P\Delta P. What matters for steering is not whether some linear separator exists in the high-dimensional residual stream, but whether the concept is aligned with the model’s own output projection.

4.3 Generalization

Cross-architecture replication.

We replicate on Llama-3.1-8B, Mistral-7B-v0.3, and Qwen2.5-7B (Table 4). The emergence pattern holds across all four architectures: zero in the first 70–80% of depth, sharp rise in the final quarter. The steering correlation is positive across all 12 model–family pairs (ρ\rho range +0.66+0.66 to +0.93+0.93). Mistral required a tokenizer-specific fix (Appendix M).

Non-transformer architectures.

We replicate the logit lens on Mamba-1.4B (48-layer SSM; Gu and Dao 2024) and RWKV-1.6B (24-layer linear attention; Peng et al. 2023). Both exhibit the same emergence pattern and final-layer drop consistent with the layer norm mismatch. Peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} closely tracks model accuracy (Table 13 in the appendix). Steering experiments on non-transformers are left for future work.

Entity steering demo.

To validate lap end-to-end, we steer London-answer prompts toward “Paris” on two architectures. On Gemma-2-2B, steering at L22 (Alin=0.20A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0.20) redirects completions (“Big Ben is located in” →\to “the heart of Paris, France”), while the middle layer L13 (Alin=0A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0) has no effect (ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P)=+0.663\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P)=+0.663, p<0.001p<0.001). On OLMo-2-1B-Instruct, steering at L13 (Alin=0.60A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0.60) produces clean redirection (“The capital of England is” →\to “Paris”), while L8 (Alin=0A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0) again fails (ρ=+0.753\rho=+0.753, p<0.001p<0.001). This is a direct comparison against the practitioner heuristic: the standard “steer at the middle layer” approach fails on both models, while lap identifies the correct layer. Full generation examples are in Appendix Q.

5 Discussion

Tuned lens comparison.

We trained tuned lenses on Pythia-2.8B, Qwen-1.5B, and Gemma-2-2B using the Muon optimizer (Jordan, 2024) on 100M tokens. The “final-layer anomaly” (AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} dropping to zero at the last layer) disappears with the tuned lens on Qwen and Pythia, confirming it is a layer norm mismatch artifact on those architectures. Gemma’s final layer behaves differently: the tuned lens does not resolve the drop, suggesting a genuinely different representation structure. For steering layer selection, the raw logit lens is the better predictor (it measures exactly what the steering mechanism uses), while the tuned lens is more informative for understanding when concepts first emerge. Full per-family comparisons are in Table 5 (Appendix B).

Connection to frontier-scale interpretability.

Concurrent work by Sofroniew et al. (2026) validates linear steering at frontier scale: 171 emotion concepts in Claude Sonnet 4.5 are representable as linear directions with causal behavioral effects. Their analysis projects steering directions through the unembedding, and finds that emotion representations concentrate in middle-to-late layers, consistent with our emergence pattern.

SAE prediction.

Our three-regime framework predicts that SAE features should be most useful for steering in regime 2. In regime 3, where the concept is already linearly accessible, SAE decomposition should add less value over difference-of-means. Testing this prediction is a natural direction for future work.

When AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} fails.

Two families have moderate AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} but low Δ​P\Delta P. Parity (Alin=0.27A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0.27, Δ​P=+0.003\Delta P=+0.003): the C⁡(d)C(d) target rank is 13,440, meaning the separation direction does not align with the “odd” token. Gender (Alin=0.50A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0.50, Δ​P=+0.012\Delta P=+0.012): C⁡(d)C(d) correctly points at “she,” but baseline probability is already ∼\sim0.4, leaving little room for improvement. These cases suggest AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} should be combined with a baseline-probability check.

Scope and limitations.

Practical guidelines for applying lap, including go/no-go thresholds and layer-selection rules, are in Appendix A. The steerability correlation includes a floor effect: concepts with Alin≈0A_{\mathrm{lin}}\approx 0 trivially have Δ​P≈0\Delta P\approx 0. The above-floor correlation (Alin>0.1A_{\mathrm{lin}}>0.1) is moderate on smaller models (ρ=+0.50\rho=+0.50 to +0.52+0.52 on Pythia-2.8B and Gemma-2-2B) and strong on larger models (ρ=+0.84\rho=+0.84 to +0.93+0.93 on Qwen-7B, Llama-8B, and Qwen-1.5B). We validated on single-token tasks because they provide the cleanest measurement setting; extensions to multi-token and distribution-level settings are discussed in Appendix C.

6 Conclusion

The logit lens, a training-free measurement, predicts where steering vectors succeed. It predicts which layer to steer at (ρ=+0.63\rho=+0.63 to +0.92+0.92) and which concepts are steerable (ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 to +0.91+0.91 across five models, with above-floor ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 on Qwen-7B). The mechanism is straightforward: the steering direction, projected through the unembedding, must assign high weight to the target token, and AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} measures exactly this. We provide a practitioner-facing diagnostic: compute AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} in one forward pass to determine whether steering is viable, at which layer, and how clean the effect will be.

Reproducibility.

All experiments use publicly available models (Gemma-2-2B, Pythia-160M/410M/1B/2.8B/6.9B, Qwen2.5-1.5B/7B, Llama-3.1-8B, Llama-3.2-1B/Instruct, Mistral-7B, OLMo-2-1B-Instruct, Mamba-1.4B, RWKV-1.6B). Experiments were conducted on a single NVIDIA RTX 3090 Ti GPU (24 GB). Total compute: primary experiments ∼\sim4 GPU-hours; steerability analysis ∼\sim2 GPU-hours per model; tuned lens training ∼\sim8 GPU-hours per model. The diagnostic tool, experimental code, and 25 controlled concept families are provided as anonymized supplementary material.

Appendix A Practical guidelines

A practitioner wanting to steer a model on a new concept faces two questions: (a) will steering work for this concept? and (b) at which layer? lap addresses both:

  1. 1.

    Compute Alin​(ℓ)A_{\mathrm{lin}}(\ell). One forward pass per prompt through the frozen model, applying the unembedding to each layer’s hidden state. No training required. Cost: LL matrix multiplications per prompt.

  2. 2.

    Will steering work? (go/no-go) If peak Alin<0.05A_{\mathrm{lin}}<0.05 across all layers, the concept is not linearly accessible and difference-of-means steering will produce negligible effects. If peak Alin>0.1A_{\mathrm{lin}}>0.1, steering is likely viable. This prediction holds across 24 controlled concept families on five models (ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 to +0.91+0.91 between peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} and max Δ​P\Delta P).

  3. 3.

    Which layer? Steer at the layer with the highest AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}. This matches or near-matches the oracle-best steering layer for 4 of 5 families on Gemma-2-2B (≥\geq99.7% of oracle Δ​P\Delta P), with within-family correlations of ρ=+0.63\rho=+0.63 to +0.92+0.92. The one miss (geography) has the weakest AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} signal (peak 0.28) and the largest probe gap.

  4. 4.

    Expect clean steering when AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is high. Concepts with high AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} achieve more on-target effect per unit of collateral damage (ρ=+0.63\rho=+0.63 to +0.65+0.65 across three models). For deployment-sensitive applications, prefer steering at layers with high AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}.

  5. 5.

    Screen on a small model. AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} on one model predicts steerability on another (ρ=+0.64\rho=+0.64 to +0.88+0.88 cross-model). Compute AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} on a small, fast model to identify promising concepts before investing compute on the target model.

  6. 6.

    What if steering is weak despite high AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}? Possible causes: (a) the steering target has too few prompts for a clean direction (ntarget<10n_{\mathrm{target}}<10); (b) the concept has many answer classes, diluting the binary contrast; (c) the model’s knowledge is split across near-synonym tokens. Examine the model’s output distribution at the recommended layer.

These thresholds are calibrated on Gemma-2-2B, Qwen-1.5B, and Pythia-2.8B and validated on Qwen-7B and Llama-8B. The emergence pattern and layer ordering are robust across models; absolute thresholds may need adjustment for larger models.

Compute cost.

lap requires one forward pass plus LL unembedding multiplications (∼\sim10% overhead). Brute-force layer search requires LL full forward passes, making lap ∼\sim30×\times cheaper for a 32-layer model.

Appendix B Tuned lens comparison

We trained tuned lenses on 100M tokens of C4 data using the Muon optimizer [Jordan, 2024]. Our Muon-trained Pythia lens produces AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} profiles that closely agree with the official EleutherAI pretrained lens (ρ=+0.94\rho=+0.94 to +0.99+0.99 across families).

Artifact resolved (Qwen, Pythia): the final-layer anomaly disappears with the tuned lens on Qwen (geography L27: raw 0.002 →\to tuned 0.576) and is neutral on Pythia. Architecture-dependent (Gemma): the tuned lens improves middle layers (geography L22: 0.260 →\to 0.698) but does not resolve the final layer, suggesting Gemma’s final layer has a genuinely different representation structure. Crystallization gap retained: the tuned lens shifts emergence earlier but does not collapse the gap between nonlinear and linear detection.

The raw logit lens matches or near-matches the oracle for 4 of 5 families. The tuned lens matches only geography. This is expected: difference-of-means steering injects a direction read out by WU∘LayerNormW_{U}\circ\text{LayerNorm}, not by a learned affine correction. The raw logit lens measures exactly what the steering mechanism uses.

Appendix C Multi-token extension

The output-alignment principle (C⁡(d)C(d) must point at the target token) operates at each autoregressive generation step. Three extensions follow naturally. (1) Per-step aggregation: compute AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} at each generation step and aggregate across the target sequence (e.g., mean or minimum). (2) First-token proxy: for many multi-token answers, the first token is discriminative (e.g., “Par” for “Paris, France”). AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} on the first token may suffice as a steerability predictor. (3) Token-set probability: measure the total probability mass the logit lens assigns to all tokens consistent with the target concept, accommodating ambiguous tokenizations. For distribution-level properties such as sentiment, AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} could be replaced by a divergence measure; the Sofroniew et al. analysis [Sofroniew et al., 2026] effectively does this at frontier scale. Our refusal demo provides preliminary evidence that the principle generalizes beyond token-level accuracy (ρ=+0.945\rho=+0.945). Systematic multi-token validation is the primary direction for future work.

Appendix D Controlled families methodology

The distinction between within-concept analysis (which uses the 5 core families without confound issues) and steerability prediction (which requires the 25 controlled binary families) reflects a broader methodological point: comparing interpretability tool effectiveness across concepts requires controlled experimental designs. When task-structure variables (answer-class count, target sizes, prompt format) vary across families, they obscure the geometric signal. We release the 25 controlled families as a reusable benchmark for future work on steerability prediction.

Appendix E Model usage summary

Appendix F Experimental details

Residual MLP probe.

The nonlinear probe is a residual MLP: h^=h+fθ​(h)\hat{h}=h+f_{\theta}(h) where fθf_{\theta} consists of LayerNorm(dd) →\to Linear(d→512d\to 512) →\to GELU →\to Dropout(0.1) →\to Linear(512→d512\to d) →\to Dropout(0.1). Total parameters: ∼\sim2.4M for Gemma-2-2B (d=2304d=2304). Trained with Adam (lr = 10−310^{-3}, weight decay = 10−410^{-4}), batch size 256, max 50 epochs with early stopping (patience = 5). The MLP and the frozen unembedding matrix together form the nonlinear probe; the unembedding weights are not updated. Training takes ∼\sim30 seconds per layer on a single GPU.

Prompt examples.

Table 7 shows representative prompts from each concept family with their correct single-token answers.

Steering target selection.

For each family, we select a steering target and compute the direction as the difference of means between target-answer and non-target-answer activations. Table 8 specifies the targets and the number of prompts in each group.

Appendix H Depth confound analysis

This appendix provides full details of the three depth-confound tests summarized in Section 4.2. See Section 4.2 for the main discussion.

  1. 1.

    Partial correlation. Pearson partial r⁡(Alin,Δ​P∣layer)=+0.507r(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P\mid\mathrm{layer})=+0.507 (p<10−9p<10^{-9}, n=130n=130). Controlling for layer index does not eliminate the relationship.

  2. 2.

    Within-family permutation. We shuffle Δ​P\Delta P values within each family independently (breaking the layer-to-Δ​P\Delta P mapping while preserving the marginal distribution per family). Of 10,000 permutations, zero produce ρ≥+0.777\rho\geq+0.777, yielding p<10−4p<10^{-4}. This test does not preserve within-family autocorrelation; the partial correlation (item 1) addresses the autocorrelation concern directly.

  3. 3.

    Restricted analysis. Among layer×\timesfamily pairs where Alin>0A_{\mathrm{lin}}>0, ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P)\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P) remains positive while ρ⁡(layer,Δ​P)\rho(\mathrm{layer},\Delta P) alone does not discriminate effective from ineffective layers in this restricted set.

Appendix I Crystallization gap

Table 10 reports the crystallization gap for each core concept family on Gemma-2-2B: the number of layers between when AmlpA_{\mathrm{mlp}} first exceeds 0.5 (the concept is nonlinearly detectable) and when AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} first exceeds 0.1 (the concept becomes output-aligned). See Section 4.1 for discussion.

Appendix J Layer-selection policy

The “Trained” column illustrates why trained probe accuracy is uninformative for steering. A logistic regression probe (5-fold cross-validated on the full 2304-dimensional residual stream) achieves >>93% classification accuracy at every layer from L0 to L25, for all five families. Yet steering at the probe’s best-accuracy layer produces near-zero Δ​P\Delta P (e.g., sequence: +0.004+0.004 vs. oracle +0.350+0.350). The probe finds some linear separator at every layer—this is expected in 2304 dimensions, where logistic regression has enough capacity to separate any two groups regardless of representation structure. What matters for steering is not whether any separator exists, but whether the concept is aligned with the model’s own output projection (AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}).

Appendix K Failure modes and perturbation sensitivity

When steering fails (the model’s top-1 prediction does not match the target), the LAP profile helps diagnose why. We compute five per-prompt features at the best-AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} layer and cluster failed prompts by kk-means (kk selected by silhouette score, range 2–5; silhouette scores 0.32–0.59). Four failure types emerge (Table 12), each with a distinct geometric signature and practical response.

The most common failure (“wrong direction,” 30–90%) reflects a model knowledge problem: the prompt’s activation projects negatively onto the steering direction, meaning the model does not encode the concept for that prompt. The “chaotic regime” failure (10–27%) is characterized by high perturbation sensitivity λ\lambda. Figure 3 shows this pattern across all layer×\timesfamily pairs: high λ\lambda coincides with near-zero steering effect, while low λ\lambda allows effective steering at layers where AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is high.

Appendix L Non-transformer replication

Table 13 reports the logit lens emergence pattern on two non-transformer architectures. The key finding: both show the same qualitative pattern as transformers—zero AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} for the first 70–80% of layers, sharp emergence in the final quarter, and a final-layer drop. Arithmetic is genuinely absent (0% model accuracy on both), and correctly shows Alin=0A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0. For the other four families, peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} closely tracks model accuracy, consistent with the transformer results. Steering experiments on non-transformers are left for future work.

Appendix M Mistral tokenizer fix

Mistral’s SentencePiece tokenizer encodes digits as two tokens (a space marker plus the digit character), while alphabetic answers (“France”, “Thursday”, “cold”) are single tokens. Our token-matching code required a Mistral-specific fix to use the last token of the encoding (the actual digit) rather than the first (the space marker). With this fix, arithmetic on Mistral achieves 64.5% model accuracy and shows the same emergence and steering patterns as the other architectures.

Appendix N Controlled concept families

Table 14 lists the 25 controlled binary concept families used for steerability prediction (Section 3.6). Each family has exactly two single-token answer classes, balanced groups (∼\sim22 items per class ×\times 4 templates ≈\approx 88 prompts per class), and consistent prompt templates. Families are sorted by peak AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} on Gemma-2-2B. Concepts with higher AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} generally show higher Δ​P\Delta P, consistent with the steerability correlations reported in Section 4.2.

Appendix O Steerability correlations and scaling

Table 15 reports steerability correlations across models. The “Controlled” row is the primary result (ρ=+0.86\rho=+0.86 to +0.91+0.91). The “above-floor” rows (restricting to families with Alin>0.05A_{\mathrm{lin}}>0.05 or >0.1>0.1) test whether the correlation survives after removing the trivial floor effect (concepts with Alin≈0A_{\mathrm{lin}}\approx 0 trivially have Δ​P≈0\Delta P\approx 0). On larger models (Qwen-7B, Llama-8B), the above-floor correlation remains strong (ρ=+0.83\rho=+0.83 to +0.93+0.93); on smaller models it weakens due to fewer above-floor data points.

Table 16 reports the scaling analysis across Pythia sizes. The number of steerable concepts grows with model size (5/23 at 160M →\to 9/23 at 6.9B), as does mean steering Δ​P\Delta P (roughly 3.4×3.4\times increase). Both plateau between 2.8B and 6.9B within the Pythia family.

Appendix P C⁡(d)C(d) analysis and steering efficiency

Table 17 reports the C⁡(d)C(d) analysis for a representative subset of concept families on Gemma-2-2B, selected to span the full range of AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} and Δ​P\Delta P values. The C⁡(d)C(d) rank indicates where the target token falls in the vocabulary when the steering direction is projected through the unembedding: rank 1 means C⁡(d)C(d) points directly at the target token (ideal for steering); a high rank means the steering direction is misaligned with the target. For example, parity has C⁡(d)C(d) rank 13,440 out of ∼\sim256K vocabulary tokens—the even/odd direction does not point at “odd” in the unembedding space, explaining why Δ​P≈0\Delta P\approx 0 despite moderate AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}.

Cross-concept correlations on Gemma-2-2B (n=27n=27: 24 controlled + 3 core families with single-token steering targets): ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P)=+0.86\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P)=+0.86; ρ⁡(C​(d)target,Δ​P)=+0.73\rho(C(d)_{\mathrm{target}},\Delta P)=+0.73; ρ⁡(‖d‖,KL)=+0.96\rho(\|d\|,\mathrm{KL})=+0.96; ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P/KL)=+0.65\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P/\mathrm{KL})=+0.65. Results replicate on Qwen-1.5B (n=26n=26: ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P)=+0.90\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P)=+0.90; ρ⁡(C⁡(d),Δ​P)=+0.78\rho(C(d),\Delta P)=+0.78; ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P/KL)=+0.65\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P/\mathrm{KL})=+0.65) and Pythia-2.8B (n=26n=26: ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P)=+0.89\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P)=+0.89; ρ⁡(C⁡(d),Δ​P)=+0.84\rho(C(d),\Delta P)=+0.84; ρ⁡(Alin,Δ​P/KL)=+0.63\rho(A_{\mathrm{lin}},\Delta P/\mathrm{KL})=+0.63).

Appendix Q Steering demos: refusal and entity redirect

Applied to refusal in Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct (40 harmful + 40 benign prompts), lap identifies layer 13 as the recommended steering layer. At layers 0–2, separability is moderate (65–88%) but steering produces zero or negative effect. At layers 8–15, both separability and steering are high.

To verify that steering produces coherent behavioral change (not just token-probability shifts), we generate full completions with the refusal direction subtracted at two layers: layer 0 (low separability, acc=0.65) and layer 13 (LAP-recommended, acc=1.0), both at α=0.5×‖d‖\alpha=0.5\times\|d\|. Table 19 shows representative examples. At layer 0, steering has no effect: completions are identical to baseline and the model continues to refuse. At layer 13, refusal is removed and the model complies. This contrast confirms that lap identifies the correct steering layer, not merely that steering works somewhere. At higher scales (α≥2.0\alpha\geq 2.0), completions degenerate into repetition, consistent with pushing the representation off the learned manifold.

Entity steering (London→\toParis).

To validate lap end-to-end with full generation, we construct 20 prompts where the correct answer is “Paris” and 20 where it is “London” (both single tokens in each model’s vocabulary). We run the experiment on two architectures: Gemma-2-2B (base, 26 layers) and OLMo-2-1B-Instruct (Allen AI, 16 layers).

On Gemma-2-2B, AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is zero at layers 0–19 and peaks at L22 (0.20). Steering Δ​P​(Paris)\Delta P(\text{Paris}) tracks AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}: ρ=+0.663\rho=+0.663 (p<0.001p<0.001). On OLMo-2-1B-Instruct, AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}} is zero at layers 0–11 and peaks at L13 (0.60), with sharper emergence and higher peak accessibility. Steering Δ​P​(Paris)\Delta P(\text{Paris}) again tracks AlinA_{\mathrm{lin}}: ρ=+0.753\rho=+0.753 (p<0.001p<0.001).

Table 20 shows generated completions on both models at three layers: the middle layer (the conventional heuristic from Turner et al. 2023, Templeton et al. 2024), the lap-recommended layer, and with α=1.0\alpha=1.0. On both models, the middle layer has Alin=0A_{\mathrm{lin}}=0 and steering produces no effect—completions are identical to baseline. At the lap-recommended layer, outputs are fully redirected to Paris. This is a direct comparison against the practitioner heuristic: the standard “steer at the middle layer” approach fails, while lap identifies the correct layer. On OLMo-2, the redirection is particularly clean: “The capital of England is” →\to “Paris”; “Big Ben is located in” →\to “Paris, 16th arrondissement”; “The British government is based in” →\to “Paris, and the French government is based in Paris.”
